title: Implementing agentic AI in customer service across complex workflows
summary: Learn how to implement agentic AI in customer service so AI agents can execute complex workflows with context, clear handoffs, and human oversight.
body_markdown:
Learn how to implement agentic AI in customer service so AI agents can execute complex workflows with context, clear handoffs, and human oversight.


A logistics team can’t keep up with customer questions about shipment delays. A financial services firm needs to escalate a compliance issue to underwriting. A manufacturing[support team](https://front.com/blog/customer-service-operations) spends too much time answering recurring order status requests.


Despite the different scenarios, the challenge is the same: Teams are spending valuable time on repetitive work. Implementing agentic AI in their customer service could help them respond faster and coordinate more effectively across conversations.


To find out where agentic AI fits into your customer service operation, explore the workflows AI agents can take on, where human judgment still matters, and how to implement them with the context, guardrails, and handoffs needed to keep work moving.


## What agentic AI means for customer service workflows


Agentic AI uses artificial intelligence to plan and take actions in pursuit of a defined goal. Unlike a chatbot, which only responds to direct prompts, an AI agent can act on its own to reach a specified goal. In a customer service context, agentic systems can interpret customer requests and take actions within defined workflows to resolve those requests.


Whereas traditional automation or chatbots usually follow scripted paths or handle narrower tasks, agentic AI is more autonomous and goal-oriented, and it can complete multi-step tasks.


Consider the aforementioned financial services team with a compliance thread in need of escalation. Agentic AI could analyze the team’s conversation, determine that the issue meets the criteria for escalation, create a detailed handoff, and keep key stakeholders informed of the status. Traditional[AI customer service software](https://front.com/blog/ai-customer-service-software) could automate individual actions like routing, but it couldn’t analyze the conversation and make the decision to escalate on its own.


## How agentic AI benefits customer service


Agentic AI offers benefits like consistent answers and efficient escalation. When you keep conversations coordinated, your team can expect other benefits of AI in customer service.


### Moves routine requests without pulling people away from high-context work


Agentic AI thrives at repetitive work like ticket intake, triage, routing, status updates, and answering frequently asked questions. A company receiving a high volume of repetitive requests could use an AI agent to automatically answer questions about shipment delays, freeing up human support specialists to work on more complex issues that require judgment and empathy.


### Keeps customer conversations intact


For teams without an omnichannel support platform, handling B2B customer conversations with multiple stakeholders is less efficient. They may have to switch between an email app, Slack, and another platform to access all the context for an issue. Today’s customer service AI tools help teams access context, summarize long conversation threads, draft responses, and coordinate next steps. A customer service representative could ask an AI agent to show them all conversations for the customer they’re supporting, or to analyze the conversation history and find a particular fact.


### Handles escalations effectively


As noted in the financial services example above, AI agents make escalations more consistent by applying predefined criteria and routing issues to the right person with all the necessary context included. The issue’s new owner can solve the problem without needing to ask the customer for more information.


### Gives teams consistent answers across channels


[AI customer service tools](https://front.com/blog/ai-for-customer-service) help teams handle higher volumes of customer questions spread across multiple communication channels. A support team handling frequent status update requests might use an AI agent to give consistent updates based on real-time access to order management systems and past conversations.


### Shows support leaders where customer work gets stuck


Beyond handling individual conversations, agentic AI systems can analyze conversation trends and operational data to identify where customer work slows down — whether escalations stall, issues go unresolved, or customers repeatedly reach out about the same problem. Leaders can solve those problems before they snowball and affect the customer experience (CX).


## Common challenges of agentic AI


AI customer service solutions can create problems when teams implement them without the right context or guardrails. For example, the agents may not have access to key customer context, or teams may try to automate too much without building in sufficient guardrails. In Front’s[Coordination Tax report](https://research.front.com/) , 71% of B2B companies using AI experienced at least one significant AI issue in the past three months.


Many of these AI failures were rooted in coordination problems. The top AI issues were additional coordination work, lost context during handoffs, and incorrect routing. Agentic AI often creates more coordination overhead when it acts without full customer context or lacks clearly defined guardrails and escalation paths. The following challenges are common in B2B.


### Poor AI-to-human handoffs


When teams rely on AI agents to make escalation and routing decisions, they need to set up clear guardrails or the agent may reassign the issue to the wrong person (or fail to hand it off altogether).


Say a financial services firm didn’t establish clear escalation rules. The AI agent then escalates the compliance thread to the wrong team, and when it finally gets to the underwriting team, it won’t include the correct context. The customer gets frustrated by the delay and the need to answer the same questions repeatedly.


### Over-automated customer interactions


Without the right guardrails, agentic AI handles complex or sensitive issues that should have been escalated to human agents.


If the financial services firm doesn’t have strong guardrails, its AI agent then tries to resolve the compliance thread itself, instead of escalating it to the underwriting team. It makes a serious mistake that frustrates the client and exposes the company to compliance risk.


### Limited visibility into how customer work moves across teams


If AI operates separately from your customer service systems, teams lose visibility into where work stands, who owns the next step, and what actions have already been taken.


Human agents may not realize an AI agent has already updated customers about shipment delays, so they spend time sending the same information again. The result is duplicated work and a confusing CX.


## How to implement agentic AI across customer service workflows


Find out how to roll out AI effectively, with real-world B2B examples of AI in customer service.


### Start with repeatable customer service workflows


[Start by automating](https://front.com/blog/customer-service-automation) low-risk, high-volume workflows. Measure them and get them right before expanding your AI tool use into more complex customer work.


A company could focus on giving its AI agent access to all the order status data it needs. Only when it verifies that the AI answers are reliable and accurate does the team expand AI usage to more complex projects.


### Set guardrails for high-context decisions


Define clear limits on what AI can handle autonomously, what requires approval, and what should stay with human teams. When the financial-services firm sets up these guardrails, its AI agent reliably escalates complex compliance threads, reducing risk and improving CX.


### Connect AI to customer conversations and operational systems


Give the AI agent the context it needs to deliver accurate answers. In B2B, agentic AI needs access to conversations across different channels, CRM data, and a company’s knowledge base.


### Create escalation paths before expanding automation


During setup, define when your tool should escalate, and specify exactly who should own different types of issues and what context should move with the request.


Strong[escalation management](https://front.com/blog/escalation-management) for the financial services team involves specifying which underwriting team members handle which types of compliance issues, and what context they need in the handoff.


### Measure operational impact beyond ticket resolution speed


When tracking the success of your AI solutions, look beyond resolution speed by tracking metrics like routing accuracy, handoff quality, repeat contacts, and customer effort. Front recommends using the[AI Experience Impact Score](https://front.com/blog/ai-experience-impact-score-axis) , a metric designed specifically for evaluating AI-supported customer interactions.


A team might find that its AI agent is giving fast responses about the shipping delays, but customer satisfaction is low, and the reopen rate is high. By looking beyond speed, the team recognizes that it needs to improve the quality of AI answers.

## FAQ


### What metrics should teams track after implementing agentic AI in customer service?


Track CX metrics like customer satisfaction and customer effort score, as well as operational metrics like response time and first contact resolution.


### What tools do teams need to implement agentic AI in customer service?


Instead of looking for standalone tools, it’s best to choose an omnichannel customer service platform like Front, which integrates agentic AI with a ticketing system, CRM, knowledge base, and other systems. That way, your AI agent can easily access customer context and conversations from all those systems to give customers more accurate responses.


### What does a realistic implementation timeline for agentic AI in customer service look like?


Implementation timelines vary depending on company size, data readiness, and the complexity of the workflows you automate, but can take a few months.
